habitat: Moister, shadier places than the other starlings: coastal towns, forest and bush, and inland riparian and lowland woodland in the north. Nomadic when not breeding. In Zimbabwe it occurs in summer only in the Rusitu–Haroni region.
summary: A common resident. The dullest glossy starling, appearing black at a distance. The female and immature are duller than the male. The adult eye runs from orange-yellow to red, and the immature eye is dark grey. Flocks warble while feeding. Newman's size line is unreadable, so the size is omitted. The page spells the name Notophilia corruscus. This list keeps Notopholia corusca. The Kemp name Blackbellied Starling and the code VB were left unchanged.

head.pattern: The dullest glossy starling, appearing black at a distance. Adult eye colour runs from orange-yellow to red.

underparts.pattern: Appears black at a distance. Female duller than the male.

head.pattern: Immature duller than the male, with a dark grey eye.

viewNotes.note: The underside in flight is not described.

calls.description: Flocks utter pleasant warbling notes while feeding. Breeding pairs make mellow trills mixed with harsher notes. The grade A call is from Grahamstown and is described as mimicking. The filename is XC285744-Black-bellied starling imitating drongo - Copy.mp3.

research.note: Newman calls it a common resident, and Avibase does not mark it rare, so all twelve months are listed. It is also described as nomadic, and as a summer bird only in one Zimbabwe locality. The size line is unreadable, so the size is omitted. The adult eye is orange-yellow to red, so no single iris colour is stored. The page spells Notophilia corruscus. No Kruger photograph was found. The grade A call is from the Eastern Cape and is labelled as mimicking. The Kemp name Blackbellied Starling and the code VB were left unchanged.

population.notes: Kemp et al. 2001 order-of-magnitude threshold 2^6=64 mature individuals (visiting breeder); paper interval half–double → 32–128.
